MOST of us have met or at least heard of the very old man who could have had his ears boxed by Napoleon, had he ever met Napoleon, which he didn't. Similarly, we know the very middle-aged person whose father might have spoken to Dr. Johnson in Fleet-street, but didn't, because he disliked the look of him; and the gracious old lady whose mother met Marie Antoinette; and the white-haired American whose father saw George Washington once, if not twice—he cannot quite remember. . .

These persons, with vague but illustrious recollections, have distinction about them—even a certain aloofness that charms us in a commonplace society. They are, it may be, in themselves nothing; by association or glamorous contact, they are much. We like them. We have occasionally spoken to them; or, rather, they have bent so far as to speak to us, in the manner of that inhabitant of the South Sea House, Lamb's Mr. Thomas Tame, if we remember rightly, whose habitual stoop and air of condensation derived from the fact of his remote and perhaps imaginary connection with the "illustrious house of Derwentwater."

But indeed these elders who could have known such seemingly distant historical personas, provide, we think, another use, in that they thrillingly remind us of the brevity of Time backwards; as we know already in our own experience of its fluidity and swiftness under our feet.

Napoleon, Marie Antoinette, Dr. Johnson, the elder and younger Pitts—how remote, how merely historical !—until indeed you come across someone who says his father knew them. That brings them near. There are two occupations that predominate the activities of the people in war time. The men are fighters, and most of the women are either farming or preparing to raise crops for at least their own household.
The raising of sufficiently large crops to feed the United States and the Allies, is one of the biggest problems of the moment.

A ball is up in Congress asking for conscription of farm workers so that the output will be at least normal. The women want to be considered as factors, and are anxious to be just as busy tiling the soil, as the men.

A number of women are studying farming at the New York State School of Agriculture at Farmingdale, Long Island, so that they will be able to teach the people how to cultivate every inch of their gardens and raise enough necessary vegetables to supply their own families. In this way the crops of the country can be diverted in a large measure to the other side and it will at the same time cut the coast of living.
